n: Psalm 105 told of God’s faithfulness; Psalm 106 confesses Israel’s unfaithfulness. It opens with ‘Hallelujah’ and a familiar refrain: God is good and his covenant love lasts forever.
No one can fully describe God’s mighty acts or praise him enough.
Happy are those who act justly and do right always — a standard Israel’s history will show they often failed to meet.
The psalmist asks to be remembered with the kindness God shows his people and to experience his salvation.
He wants to share in the prosperity and joy of God’s chosen people.
Confession begins: ‘We have sinned with our fathers.’ He includes his own generation, not just blaming the past. The three verbs echo Solomon’s and Daniel’s confessions.

f.w: We have sinned with our fathers

n: In Egypt the ancestors failed to grasp God’s wonders and rebelled at the Red Sea, complaining when Pharaoh’s army appeared.
Yet God saved them anyway — ‘for his name’s sake,’ to show his power and keep his word, not because they deserved it.
At God’s rebuke the sea dried up, and he led them through the deep as easily as walking across open country.
God rescued them from the enemy — ‘redeemed’ them, as a kinsman buys back a relative.
The returning waters covered the Egyptian army; not one survived.
Then they believed and sang his praise — the Song of Moses.
But they quickly forgot and did not wait for God’s guidance. Gratitude faded fast.
They craved food intensely in the wilderness and put God to the test.
God gave them the quail they demanded but sent a wasting disease among them. Getting what we want is not always a blessing.
Some were jealous of the leadership of Moses and of Aaron, the priest set apart (‘saint’) for the Lord.

f.g: Holy one; one consecrated to God.

n: In Korah’s rebellion, the ground opened and swallowed the rebels Dathan and Abiram with their households.
Fire from the Lord consumed the 250 men who had offered incense in defiance.
At Horeb (Sinai), while Moses was on the mountain, they made and worshipped a metal calf.

f.g: An idol made of melted, cast metal.

n: A bitter irony: they traded the glorious God for the statue of a grass-eating ox.
They forgot God their Savior, who had worked great deeds in Egypt.
Those deeds were wonders in ‘the land of Ham’ (Egypt) and awe-inspiring acts at the Red Sea.
God would have destroyed them, but Moses ‘stood in the breach’ — like a soldier filling a gap in a broken wall — to plead for them. Moses foreshadows Christ the Intercessor.

f.w: stood before him in the breach

n: At the edge of the promised land, they rejected the ‘pleasant land’ and doubted God’s promise after the spies’ report.
They grumbled in their tents and refused to listen to the Lord.
So God raised his hand in an oath that they would die in the wilderness.

f.w: lifted up his hand against them

n: He also warned their descendants would be scattered among the nations if they kept rebelling — later fulfilled in exile.

f.w: to scatter them in the lands

n: At Peor in Moab they joined in worship of the Baal of that place and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless idols.

f.g: Offerings to lifeless gods, or rites for the dead.

n: Their actions provoked God, and a plague broke out among them.
Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, stepped in and acted against the open sin, and the plague stopped.
His zeal was credited to him as righteousness, and God gave him a covenant of lasting priesthood.
At Meribah, ‘the waters of strife,’ the people’s complaints led even Moses into trouble.
They embittered his spirit so that he spoke rashly — and Moses was not allowed to enter the land.
In Canaan, they failed to remove the idolatrous nations as God had commanded.

f.w: They did not destroy the nations

n: Instead they intermarried with them and copied their practices.
They worshipped the Canaanite idols, which became a trap.
Worst of all, they sacrificed their own children to demons — the false gods behind the idols.

f.g: Hebrew shedim, demons or false spirits.

n: They shed innocent blood, killing their own children for Canaan’s idols, and defiled the land itself.

f.w: the land was polluted with blood

n: Their deeds made them unclean. Idolatry is pictured as spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to their covenant ‘husband,’ God.

f.g: Committed spiritual adultery — idolatry as covenant betrayal.

n: God’s anger burned so fiercely that he loathed his own people’s behavior.
He handed them over to foreign nations, and their enemies ruled them — the repeated cycle of the book of Judges.

f.w: gave them into the hand of the heathen

n: They were crushed and humbled under their oppressors.
Again and again God rescued them, but they kept choosing rebellion and sinking lower.

f.w: Many times did he deliver them

n: Still God noticed their distress and heard their cry.
He remembered his covenant and relented because of his abundant love. ‘Repented’ here means he turned from punishment to mercy.
God even caused their captors to treat them with compassion.

f.w: made them also to be pitied

n: The final prayer: save us and gather us from among the nations so we can praise you again. This fits the exile; Latter-day Saints see it echoed in the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.w: gather us from among the heathen
f.r: 1 Chronicles 16:35; Deuteronomy 30:3-4; 1 Nephi 10:14; Articles of Faith 1:10

n: This doxology closes Book Four of the Psalms (Psalms 90–106). All the people respond, ‘Amen. Hallelujah.’

f.w: let all the people say, Amen
